title: Implement vector search on Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL

questions.q: How many dimensions does Azure OpenAI's text-embedding-ada-002 model produce?

options.why: 505 is the flat index dimension limit.
4,096 is the quantizedFlat and diskANN dimension limit.
Correct. ada-002 produces 1,536-dimensional vectors.
3,072 is text-embedding-3-large.

questions.hint: This model's dimension count is also the default in the vector embedding policy.
questions.explain: The dimensions in the vector policy must match the embedding model.

questions.q: Your container stores normalized Azure OpenAI embeddings for a support knowledge base. Which distance function does Learn recommend?

options.text: hamming
options.why: Not a supported distance function.

options.text: manhattan
options.why: Not a supported distance function.

options.text: cosine
options.why: Correct. Cosine handles normalized embeddings well and gives intuitive scores.

options.text: euclidean
options.why: Euclidean suits cases where magnitude matters; it's less common for text embeddings.

questions.hint: Normalized embeddings compare well by angle. Which function measures angle?
questions.explain: Supported: cosine (default), dotproduct, euclidean.

questions.q: A container holds 3 million product embeddings with 1,536 dimensions. Which vector index type fits best?

options.text: flat
options.why: flat supports only up to 505 dimensions.

options.text: A range index on /embedding
options.why: Range indexes don't help embedding arrays; exclude them.

options.text: quantizedFlat
options.why: quantizedFlat is recommended up to about 50,000 vectors per physical partition.

options.text: diskANN
options.why: Correct. DiskANN gives the best performance for millions of vectors, up to 4,096 dimensions.

questions.hint: Millions of high-dimension vectors need approximate search built for scale.
questions.explain: flat for small/exact, quantizedFlat for moderate sizes, diskANN for large datasets.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. You plan to add vector search to an existing `products` container that already has data.

rows.text: You can add a vector embedding policy to the existing container.
rows.why: Vector policies must be set at creation, and vector search is only supported on new containers.

rows.text: The account needs the vector search feature enabled first.
rows.why: Enable Vector Search for NoSQL API or EnableNoSQLVectorSearch.

rows.text: The feature must be requested through a support ticket and manually approved.
rows.why: It's auto-approved; it might take 15 minutes to take effect.

rows.text: Storing embeddings as float16 instead of float32 halves vector storage.
rows.why: float16 reduces storage by 50%.

questions.hint: Vector policies are set when a container is created, and the account feature comes first.
questions.explain: Plan vector policies before creating the container.

questions.q: Write costs are high on a vector container, and the indexing policy includes `/*` with no exclusions. What change does Learn recommend?

options.text: Add the embedding path to excludedPaths
options.why: Correct. Embedding arrays don't benefit from range indexes; including them wastes storage and raises write costs.

options.text: Change dataType from float32 to uint8
options.why: uint8 needs quantized embeddings and doesn't remove range indexing.

options.text: Disable automatic indexing for the container
options.why: Turning off indexing breaks your filter queries.

options.text: Switch the vector index from diskANN to flat
options.why: flat can't index 1,536 dimensions and doesn't fix range indexing.

questions.hint: Indexing every path includes a huge array that nobody filters on.
questions.explain: Exclude the embedding path from standard range indexes and index it with a vector index instead.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A new container has a quantizedFlat index on `/embedding` and holds 300 vectors so far.

rows.text: The quantizedFlat index is fully effective at this size.
rows.why: quantizedFlat and diskANN need at least 1,000 vectors before the index becomes effective.

rows.text: Queries may fall back to full scans and cost more RUs until more vectors are added.
rows.why: With fewer than 1,000 vectors, queries fall back to full scans.

rows.text: The same policy can also index a second path, /titleEmbedding.
rows.why: Multiple vector paths can be defined in one policy.

questions.hint: Approximate indexes need a minimum number of vectors before they help.
questions.explain: Index types need enough vectors; multiple embedding paths are supported.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. You write a vector embedding policy for /embedding and leave out dataType, dimensions and distanceFunction.

rows.text: The distance function defaults to cosine.
rows.why: cosine is the default distanceFunction.

rows.text: The dimensions default to 1,536.
rows.why: 1,536 is the default, which matches text-embedding-ada-002.

rows.text: The data type defaults to int8 to save storage.
rows.why: The default dataType is float32.

questions.hint: The defaults match a common Azure OpenAI embedding model at full precision.
questions.explain: Vector embedding policy defaults: dataType float32, dimensions 1,536, distanceFunction cosine. Dimensions must match your embedding model.

questions.q: A team creates a container with a flat vector index for 1,536-dimension embeddings, because they want exact results. The policy is rejected. Why?

options.text: Exact search needs the diskANN index
options.why: diskANN is approximate. Exact search is what flat (or brute force) gives.

options.text: The flat index supports at most 505 dimensions
options.why: Correct. flat gives 100 percent recall but limits vectors to 505 dimensions.

options.text: The flat index needs at least 1,000 vectors before you create it
options.why: The 1,000-vector minimum is about quantizedFlat and diskANN being effective, not about creating flat.

options.text: Flat indexes support only the euclidean distance function
options.why: The distance function isn't the problem. The dimension count is.

questions.hint: Each index type has a maximum number of dimensions. flat's is much lower than the others.
questions.explain: flat stores vectors in the main index with exact brute-force search and 100 percent recall, but limits vectors to 505 dimensions. quantizedFlat and diskANN support up to 4,096.

questions.q: Storage for 40 million float32 embeddings is getting expensive. Tests show that lower precision barely changes search quality. Which change does Learn suggest first?

options.text: Switch the distance function to euclidean
options.why: The distance function changes scoring, not storage size.

options.text: Switch the vector dataType to float16
options.why: Correct. float16 cuts vector storage by 50 percent with minimal impact on quality for most AI apps.

options.text: Reduce the dimensions in the policy without changing the model
options.why: Dimensions must match the embedding model, or inserts fail.

options.text: Remove the vector index and rely on full scans
options.why: That makes every query far more expensive.

questions.hint: Precision and storage trade off. Which data type halves the size of each number?
questions.explain: float32 gives full precision but uses the most storage. float16 reduces storage by 50 percent with minimal impact on quality. int8/uint8 need quantized embeddings.

questions.q: Your embeddings come from Azure OpenAI and are guaranteed to be normalized. You want the same ranking as cosine with slightly cheaper computation. Which distance function fits?

options.text: dotproduct
options.why: Correct. For normalized vectors, dot product gives the same results as cosine and can be slightly faster.

options.text: manhattan
options.why: Manhattan isn't a supported distance function. The options are cosine, dotproduct and euclidean.

options.text: euclidean
options.why: Euclidean measures straight-line distance and is described for specialized cases.

options.text: cosine, because it's the only option for Azure OpenAI
options.why: cosine works, but dotproduct is also valid for normalized vectors and can be faster.

questions.hint: For unit-length vectors, two of the functions rank results identically.
questions.explain: Dot product measures angle and magnitude. For normalized vectors, it's mathematically identical to cosine similarity but can be slightly faster to compute.

questions.q: A RAG app passes retrieved documents to a language model as context. How many results does Learn suggest returning?

options.text: All matching documents
options.why: Returning everything is slow and expensive.
Correct. Five to ten results give context without overwhelming the model.
Too few results can miss needed context.
More context doesn't always help and raises token costs.

questions.hint: RAG needs enough context to answer, but not so much that the prompt fills with noise.
questions.explain: RAG 5–10, user search 10–20 with pagination, recommendations 3–5.

questions.q: Documents were embedded with text-embedding-ada-002. A developer embeds user queries with a different model to save cost, and results become irrelevant. Why?

options.text: The cosine distance function works with ada-002 embeddings alone
options.why: Cosine works with any embeddings; the problem is the mismatch.

options.text: Different models create incompatible vector spaces
options.why: Correct. Use the same model for queries and documents.

options.text: The query vector belongs inline, not in a parameter
options.why: Parameters are recommended and don't cause this.

options.text: The vector index has to be rebuilt after each query
options.why: Indexes aren't rebuilt per query.

questions.hint: Vectors from different models live in different spaces.
questions.explain: Query embeddings must come from the same model that produced the document embeddings.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A query uses `VectorDistance(c.embedding, @queryVector)` with cosine distance.

rows.text: A document scoring 0.9 is more similar to the query than one scoring 0.5.
rows.why: With cosine, higher scores mean greater similarity.

rows.text: Adding WHERE VectorDistance(c.embedding, @queryVector) > 0.7 keeps highly similar results.
rows.why: A 0.7 threshold typically returns highly relevant results.

rows.text: Omitting TOP N is fine because the index limits the results automatically.
rows.why: Without TOP N the query tries to return all documents.

questions.hint: Cosine similarity: higher is closer. TOP N still matters.
questions.explain: Use TOP N, ORDER BY VectorDistance, and optional thresholds.

questions.q: An evaluation job must compare approximate DiskANN results against exact results for 200 test queries. How do you get exact results?

options.text: Remove TOP N so that every document gets compared
options.why: Removing TOP N returns everything; it doesn't change the search method.

options.text: Switch the distance function from cosine to euclidean
options.why: The distance function doesn't make search exact.

options.text: Rebuild the container with a flat index
options.why: flat can't hold 1,536 dimensions, and rebuilding isn't needed.

options.text: Pass true as the third argument to VectorDistance
options.why: Correct. true forces brute-force search for 100% accurate results.

questions.hint: VectorDistance takes more than two arguments.
questions.explain: Reserve brute force for evaluation and testing or very small datasets.

questions.q: Vector queries for a user-facing search page are slow and costly. Which two changes follow Learn's optimization guidance? (Select two.)

options.text: Request TOP 10 instead of TOP 100 when the page shows 10
options.why: Correct. Use the smallest reasonable TOP N.

options.text: Force brute-force search for more accurate ranking
options.why: Brute force consumes far more RUs and adds latency.

options.text: Embed the 1,536 numbers directly in the query text
options.why: Inline vectors are unwieldy and lose plan caching.

options.text: Project id, title and score instead of SELECT *
options.why: Correct. Project only needed fields.

questions.hint: Return fewer results and fewer properties.
questions.explain: Limit results, project fields, use partition keys, and pick the right index type.

questions.q: Users search for exact error codes such as 0x80070005 as well as plain-language descriptions. Which query approach does Learn recommend?

options.text: Brute-force VectorDistance with true as the third argument
options.why: Exact vector math still doesn't match exact codes.

options.text: A cosine similarity threshold of 0.9 in the WHERE clause
options.why: A threshold filters results; it doesn't add keyword matching.

options.text: Hybrid search: RRF over VectorDistance and FullTextScore
options.why: Correct. RRF merges semantic and keyword rankings.

options.text: Plain vector search, with TOP N raised to 100 results
options.why: More vector results don't add exact keyword matching.

questions.hint: Exact codes need keyword matching, and descriptions need meaning. Combine both rankings.
questions.explain: Hybrid search combines vector similarity with full-text scoring through Reciprocal Rank Fusion.

questions.q: A hybrid query uses `RRF(VectorDistance(…), FullTextScore(…), [1, 3])`. What does the weight array do?

options.text: Full-text score counts three times as much as vector similarity
options.why: Correct. Weights map in order: vector 1, full-text 3.

options.text: Limits the query to partitions 1 and 3
options.why: Weights have nothing to do with partitions.

options.text: Vector similarity counts three times as much as full-text
options.why: Weights follow the order of the scoring functions, so it's the reverse.

options.text: Returns 1 vector result and 3 full-text results per query
options.why: Weights influence ranking, not result counts.

questions.hint: The weights array scales each ranking's contribution.
questions.explain: Use higher full-text weight when users search for codes, names and exact terms.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A vector query asks for TOP 10 with a filter that excludes most documents.

rows.text: With post-filtering, the query might return fewer than 10 results.
rows.why: If top matches fail the filter, fewer rows come back.

rows.text: Selective filters can improve performance by reducing the vectors compared.
rows.why: Pre-filtering shrinks the search space.

rows.text: You choose pre- or post-filtering with a query hint for every query.
rows.why: The query optimizer chooses automatically based on selectivity.

rows.text: Post-filtering always returns exactly the number of results requested in TOP.
rows.why: Post-filtering can return fewer results if top matches fail the filter.

questions.hint: Post-filtering can leave you short. Selective filters reduce work.
questions.explain: Filters and vector search work together; the optimizer picks the strategy.

questions.q: You try a hybrid query, but it fails because the container was configured only with a vector policy and a diskANN index. What else is required?

options.text: A second vector path for /content in the vector policy
options.why: Another vector path doesn't enable FullTextScore.

options.text: Changing the distance function to dotproduct
options.why: Distance function doesn't enable full-text scoring.

options.text: A flat index in place of the diskANN vector index
options.why: Index type isn't the issue, and flat can't hold large dimensions.

options.text: A full-text policy and full-text indexes on the text paths
options.why: Correct. Hybrid search needs a full-text policy and fullTextIndexes as well as vector indexes.

questions.hint: Full-text scoring needs its own policy and index.
questions.explain: Configure fullTextPaths in the full-text policy and fullTextIndexes in the indexing policy.

questions.q: A vector query filters to one category of 1,000 documents out of 100,000. The optimizer applies the filter before comparing vectors. What's the effect?

options.text: Only those 1,000 documents are compared, which improves efficiency
options.why: Correct. Pre-filtering reduces the search space before vector comparison.

options.text: The query returns fewer than TOP N results by design
options.why: That risk belongs to post-filtering, not pre-filtering.

options.text: The filter is ignored because vector queries can't filter
options.why: Vector queries can combine with metadata filters.

options.text: All 100,000 are ranked first, and then the filter removes most of them
options.why: That describes post-filtering.

questions.hint: Before or after: when is the filter applied, and how many vectors are compared?
questions.explain: Pre-filtering reduces the search space before vector comparison, which helps with selective filters. Post-filtering ranks first, preserving ranking quality but sometimes returning fewer results than requested.

questions.q: A team plans to use hybrid search (VectorDistance plus FullTextScore) for every query, including ones where pure vector search already works well. What does Learn advise?

options.text: Avoid hybrid search, because RRF can't weight the two rankings
options.why: RRF accepts a weights array.

options.text: Use hybrid search only where it adds clear value, because it costs more
options.why: Correct. Hybrid search evaluates both scoring functions, so use it when it helps.

options.text: Use hybrid everywhere, because it always improves relevance at no extra cost
options.why: Evaluating two scoring functions costs more.

options.text: Use hybrid search only on containers with a flat index
options.why: Hybrid search doesn't depend on the flat index.

questions.hint: Combining two scoring functions means doing two kinds of work.
questions.explain: Hybrid search costs more because it evaluates both VectorDistance and FullTextScore. Use it when it provides clear value, such as queries mixing exact terms and meaning.

questions.q: What does the change feed processor store in the lease container?

options.text: The embeddings generated for each document
options.why: Embeddings are written back to the documents.

options.text: The vector index for the monitored container's embeddings
options.why: Vector indexes live in the data container's indexing policy.

options.text: Partition ownership and the checkpoint for each partition
options.why: Correct. Leases track which instance owns each partition and its checkpoint.

options.text: Copies of every changed document, kept for replay
options.why: The change feed itself records changes; leases don't copy documents.

questions.hint: The lease container is how processor instances share work and remember progress.
questions.explain: Leases give checkpointing, coordination across instances and failover.

questions.q: Editors fix typos in metadata fields many times a day, and each change triggers an expensive embedding call. How should you reduce cost?

options.text: Re-embed only when a stored content hash changes
options.why: Correct. Selective refresh skips changes that don't affect semantic content.

options.text: Turn off the change feed for that container
options.why: You'd lose embedding refresh entirely.

options.text: Switch from the push model to the pull model
options.why: Pull changes when you read, not whether you re-embed.

options.text: Increase the lease container to 4,000 RU/s
options.why: Lease throughput doesn't reduce embedding API calls.

questions.hint: Not every edit changes the text that was embedded.
questions.explain: Store a hash of the embedded text and refresh only when it differs.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A team plans embedding refresh with the Cosmos DB change feed.

rows.text: The change feed must be turned on for each container before use.
rows.why: It's enabled by default on all containers.

rows.text: Changes within one partition key arrive in modification order.
rows.why: Ordered delivery within a partition key.

rows.text: The pull model stores progress in the lease container automatically.
rows.why: With pull, you keep the continuation token yourself.

questions.hint: The change feed is on by default. Order is per partition key. Pull doesn't use leases.
questions.explain: Push uses leases and automatic checkpoints; pull uses continuation tokens you store.

questions.q: Two Azure Functions both monitor the knowledge-base container: one refreshes embeddings and one updates a search log. They should share one lease container. What must differ?

options.text: Their leaseContainerPrefix values
options.why: Correct. Functions monitoring the same container can share a lease container with different prefixes.

options.text: The partition keys they read from
options.why: Both read the same data container's partitions.

options.text: The database names they connect to
options.why: They use the same database.

options.text: The embedding models they call
options.why: Embedding models aren't related to lease sharing.

questions.hint: Two processors can share a lease container if their leases don't collide.
questions.explain: Share a lease container with different leaseContainerPrefix values, or use separate lease containers.

questions.q: You're building production embedding refresh from the change feed and want reliable delivery with little operational code. Which consumption model does Learn recommend?

options.text: The push model, using Azure Functions or the change feed processor
options.why: Correct. Push delivers changes to your code and handles progress, which is simpler and more reliable for production.

options.text: Enabling the change feed on each container first
options.why: The change feed is enabled by default on all containers.

options.text: A nightly full scan of the container
options.why: A scan reprocesses everything and misses the point of the change feed.

options.text: The pull model with a loop that polls every second
options.why: Pull gives more control, but you manage polling and progress yourself.

questions.hint: One model sends changes to you. The other makes you go and ask.
questions.explain: For embedding refresh in production, the push model (Azure Functions or the change feed processor library) provides better reliability and simpler operations. Use pull for batch scenarios or more control.
